q: In the book's landscape table, which systems are self-hosted and have full identity file support?
explanation: Only OpenClaw and NanoClaw get full marks for structured identity files while being self-hosted. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1.1)

q: How does default host access differ between OpenClaw and NanoClaw?
options: OpenClaw has full filesystem access by default; NanoClaw isolates work in containers
Both isolate every task by default
NanoClaw has full host access; OpenClaw uses containers
explanation: OpenClaw relies on opt-in restrictions; NanoClaw is isolation-first by architecture. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1)

q: A team wants to move its OpenClaw SOUL.md and AGENTS.md to NanoClaw. What does the book say about the identity layer?
options: NanoClaw does not support identity files
Files must be rewritten as container specs
explanation: The comparison lists NanoClaw's behavioral identity layer as compatible with OpenClaw's. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1)

q: Why does the book rate NanoClaw's configuration complexity higher than OpenClaw's?
explanation: Container specifications add setup work, along with container spin-up overhead per tool call. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1)

q: A Python-skilled team needs a multi-step task pipeline with defined start and end states and no always-on runtime. Which does the book point to?
explanation: Python frameworks are better instrumented for pipelines and skip the cost of maintaining a persistent runtime. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.6)

q: For an always-on assistant that reacts to events and keeps context across sessions, which does the book say provide the full runtime model?
explanation: The others are libraries, builders, or hosted assistants rather than always-on runtimes. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.6)

q: A technical team with no developers wants to configure an agent without writing code. Why does the book favor OpenClaw or NanoClaw here?
options: They have no configuration at all
They are configured through JSON and markdown files
They are managed by a cloud provider
explanation: Python frameworks need Python expertise. The book calls this team skill fit often a bigger constraint than architecture. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.6)

q: How does the book position LangChain and LlamaIndex?
options: As developer frameworks for building custom agents, not deployable runtimes
explanation: They are a framework layer. LangChain targets general agent and RAG pipelines; LlamaIndex targets document-heavy RAG. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1.1)

q: Which two systems does the landscape table position as no-code builders?
explanation: Dify is listed as a no-code agent builder and Flowise as a no-code LangChain builder. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1.1)

q: When does the book recommend n8n with AI nodes?
options: For research experiments with many agents
When a workflow automation backbone with AI in certain steps beats a pure agent
When structured identity files are required
explanation: n8n suits hybrid automation. The table shows it has no native identity files or built-in memory. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1.1)

q: Why do Claude.ai Projects and OpenAI Assistants get only partial credit for identity files?
options: They use project instructions or a system prompt rather than structured multi-file identity
explanation: The book reserves full credit for separate SOUL.md/AGENTS.md-style files that support its governance model. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1.1)

q: Which entry in the landscape table is a commercial, non-self-hosted option aimed at enterprise development teams?
explanation: The table marks AWS Kiro as managed and commercial. OpenClaw and NanoClaw are the self-hosted alternatives. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §11.1.1)
